title: How the Quantum Sorites Phenomenon Strengthens the Bell Argument and How a Random-Matrix Collapse Dynamics Answers It
abstract: Bell proved that no theory of pre-existing local values can reproduce the predictions of quantum mechanics, but his proof leaves the culprit ambiguous: one may reject either of two independence conditions, Outcome Independence or Parameter Independence, and most commentators have found Outcome Independence the safer sacrifice. The first part of this paper presents, in a form adapted to spin-1/2 particles in the singlet state, an argument (Forster 2014) that removes the ambiguity: using a chained family of experiments in which quantum mechanics predicts an extreme pattern of correlations -- the quantum Sorites phenomenon -- a contradiction is derived without ever assuming Outcome Independence. Under the resulting theorem, anyone who holds that hidden variables could improve on the quantum probabilities must give up Parameter Independence itself. That looks like a heavy price, because Parameter Independence appears to be protected twice over: rejecting it seems to put superluminal influences into spacetime, and its statistical shadow -- the No-Signaling condition -- is experimentally beyond reproach The second part of the paper shows that the price is payable. In the random-matrix collapse dynamics proposed by Kryukov, measurement is a random walk of the quantum state, and the hidden variable is not a stock of values fixed at the source but the random stream that drives the walk -- like the stored random numbers of a computer simulation, with the measurement settings playing the role of seeds. In that framework Parameter Independence is false while Outcome Independence and No-Signaling are both true, and one can say exactly how the Sorites argument is blocked, why the violation involves no process propagating in spacetime, and why the influence of one wing's setting on the other wing's outcome -- demonstrated here in a simulation -- can never be used to send a message.
summary: This paper advances Bell's theorem by using the 'quantum Sorites phenomenon' to show that local hidden variable theories must reject Parameter Independence. It then proposes a random-matrix collapse model where this violation occurs naturally, resolving the conflict with special relativity while preserving the experimentally robust No-Signaling condition.
main_problem: To strengthen Bell's theorem by deriving a contradiction without assuming Outcome Independence, thereby forcing hidden variable theories to reject Parameter Independence.
main_result: The quantum Sorites phenomenon forces any local hidden variable theory that improves upon quantum predictions to abandon Parameter Independence (PI). A random-matrix collapse model shows this violation is possible while preserving No-Signaling.
method: The paper uses a chained family of experiments (Sorites argument) combined with a novel stochastic dynamics model (random-matrix collapse) to test the assumptions underlying Bell's theorem.
model_or_system: The system involves spin-1/2 particles in the singlet state measured at two distant locations. The theoretical framework uses random walks driven by independent, fixed random streams ($\lambda$) to model measurement collapse dynamics.
key_observables:
Correlation probabilities $P(X 
eq Y)$ across a chain of settings; violation of Parameter Independence (PI); maintenance of No-Signaling (NS).
important_parameters: Measurement angles ($a, b$); the degree of correlation change ($\Delta$); the structure of the random matrix ensemble.
main_assumptions: The initial argument assumes standard autonomy; the model assumes measurement is a stochastic random walk driven by fixed hidden streams $\lambda$.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the quantum Sorites phenomenon via chained measurements. Figure 2 shows the quadratic dependence of correlation on angle difference. Figure 3 simulates setting-dependent outcome jumps (violating PI) while maintaining average statistics (preserving NS).
paper_structure: Part 1 establishes the Stronger Theorem using the quantum Sorites argument to target PI directly. Part 2 introduces the random-matrix collapse dynamics, showing how this framework violates PI deterministically while keeping OI and NS true.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, relativity-respecting mechanism (random state evolution) for violating Parameter Independence, which is a major conceptual hurdle in interpreting Bell tests.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: The quantum Sorites phenomenon arises from a chained family of measurement settings on singlet pairs. Solid links join adjacent settings (ε apart), where the recorded bits agree with probability approaching one; the dashed closing link joins the two ends of the chain, where the settings differ by 180◦and the bits disagree with certainty.

Figure 2: The quantum probability of a mismatch between the recorded bits as a function of the difference in measurement angles, sin2(∆/2), and its Extreme Non-classical idealization: no mismatches until the settings are fully opposed, then certain mismatch. The quadratic flatness at small angles is what allows a chain of N near-certainties to remain a near-certainty jointly.

Figure 3: The simulation. (a) Fixed stream λ, swept setting b: the joint outcome (1–0 = Bob up–Alice down, 0–1 = the reverse) holds steady over stretches of b and then jumps — roughly thirty jumps as b sweeps from 0◦to 180◦— and the jump pattern differs erratically from stream to stream (λ1, λ2, λ3). Zooming in on the marked jump, again and again, always finds the same thing: a b below which the outcome is one way and a b above which it is the other, boxed here inside an interval of 1.5 × 10−11 degrees.
